Bass River, New Jersey. Route 542 near Loveland Lane, Sunday October 11, 2026, about 10 PM.

A couple was taking a night drive through the Pine Barrens with their kids asleep in the back seat. It was dark and raining. As they came around the bend where Loveland Lane meets Route 542, their high beams lit up a massive figure stepping out from the right side of the road.

She hit the brakes. She describes it as about eight feet tall, bulky, with a giant frame and jet black fur that looked soaking wet, the headlights reflecting off it. Human like hands. Unusually long arms that swung with a heavy reach. It walked with a slight hunch, but so fast it almost looked like it was gliding. A few steps and it had cleared the road and vanished into the dark. She asked her husband if he saw it too. He did.

They were shaken enough to call the New Jersey State Park Police and the NJDEP when they got home. Both said they do not handle that kind of thing, and the NJDEP pointed them to the BFRO.

A week later two BFRO investigators met them at the bend. They found a well used game trail on both sides of the road, some broken branches and a few unclear impressions, nothing they could tie to the sighting after a very rainy fall. A recreation put the look at four to five seconds, and a nearby telephone pole put the height at about seven and a half to eight feet. The investigators say the witnesses kept scanning the woods the whole time and did not want to leave the group.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=82683

Denver, Colorado. Cheesman Park, Capitol Hill.

Before it was an eighty acre city park with a pavilion and views of the Front Range, this ground was Mount Prospect and then Denver City Cemetery. In the 1890s Congress let Denver turn the cemetery into a park. The city hired undertaker E.P. McGovern to move the dead to Riverside. He was fired after The Denver Republican reported he was breaking bodies apart and packing pieces into multiple caskets to bill more per coffin. The city stopped the dig. Estimates say about 1,500 to 3,000 people were left under what became Cheesman Park.

For more than a century, people have told stories about cold spots, sunken coffin shaped rectangles in the grass, the smell of roses out of season, and figures that do not belong on a picnic lawn. This Halloween those stories are also a business. Guides like Will Olson of Denver Local Tours walk groups through the park for about twenty eight dollars, promising eternal residents still buried underfoot. Bike and bar crawls start at the pavilion. Colorado Sun reporters watched the crowds and then asked archivists and rival guides whether it is right to profit from people who cannot consent.

Olson argues the city already commodified them when it turned a cemetery into a park. Historian guide Phil Goodstein says a lot of the ghost lore is dubious and that national companies have crowded local operators. Aspen archivist Anna Lookabill draws a harder line. Cemetery tours can teach real history, she says, without selling bunk paranormal claims.

Unmarked graves under a city lawn, or the most honest haunted park in America because the bodies never left?

Source: https://coloradosun.com/2026/10/31/halloween-tours-denver-cheesman-park-ethical-concerns/

Loveland, Ohio. Along the Little Miami River, the Frogman will not leave town.

Top 5 things to know about the Loveland Frogman:

1) The legend usually starts in May 1955, when a businessman driving through Loveland late at night reported three frog or lizard faced bipeds, about three to four feet tall, by the side of the road. In some tellings one held a wand like device that threw sparks.

2) The story went quiet for years, then came back hard in March 1972. Loveland police officer Ray Shockey reported seeing an unidentified animal on Riverside Drive near the Totes boot factory, roughly three to four feet tall, that scrambled over a guardrail toward the river.

3) Days later, officer Mark Matthews said he saw a similar animal in the same area, shot it, and identified it as a large tailless iguana, about three to three and a half feet long, likely an escaped pet. He later called the more dramatic Frogman retellings a hoax built on that carcass.

4) That has not stopped the folklore. Loveland still leans into the Frogman with local art, tours, and a festival, and later witnesses still claim frog like bipeds near the river and roads around town.

5) Folklorists put the creature in the same family as other mid century roadside humanoids. Skeptics point to the iguana, misidentified wildlife, and a story that got bigger every time it was retold. Believers say the 1955 account and Shockey's first report never needed an iguana to be strange.

Escaped pet, local mascot, or something that still climbs the guardrail after dark?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loveland_frog

Flatwoods, West Virginia. September 12, 1952. A light fell on a hill, and a town got a monster.

Top 5 things to know about the Flatwoods Monster:

1) Around 7:15 PM on September 12, 1952, boys in Flatwoods, Braxton County, saw a bright object streak across the sky and appear to land on a nearby hillside. Kathleen May and several of the boys went up to investigate.

2) They reported a tall figure with a glowing red face, a dark green body, claw like hands, and a pointed or spade shaped hood or headpiece. Some accounts put it at about ten to twelve feet. It hissed, and witnesses said it seemed to float or glide rather than walk.

3) The group fled. Several later said they felt sick afterward. Searchers reported a pungent mist or odor in the area and found a circular flattened area of grass and skid like marks on the ground.

4) Newspapers from West Virginia to Washington picked up the story within days. It became known as the Flatwoods Monster or the Braxton County Monster, and it is still one of the most famous close encounter cases of the early flying saucer era.

5) Skeptical explanations have included a meteor fireball, the landing light of an aircraft, and a barn owl in a tree whose shape, plus fear and a bad smell from vegetation, got turned into a hooded giant. Believers still point to the multiple witnesses and the ground traces.

A scared look at an owl in the dark, or something that landed on a West Virginia hill and never came back?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatwoods_monster

North Liberty, Iowa. October 13, 2026, about 5:17 PM.

A driver heading home from work was traveling north on Alexander Way toward the stop sign at 240th Street NE when a red Chevrolet pickup stopped ahead at the intersection. Across the open cornfield, high in the daytime sky, a large smooth pill shaped object was moving right to left. Dull white gray, almost smoky, solid looking, with rounded edges and no wings, tail, or other aircraft features. It held altitude and did not tumble. The witness watched it for about a minute.

Then a strange rainbow colored shape appeared ahead of the capsule. It looked like a small square with rounded corners, a little larger than the capsule, and it seemed to stay put while its colors swirled. About ten seconds later the capsule reached it and appeared to pass into or through it. At that exact moment both objects disappeared, with no cloud to hide behind and no sound from inside the car.

The pickup driver got out, looked straight at the witness, and asked, "Did you see that?" The answer was yes. He said "OK," got back in, and looked shaken. The witness lives near an airport and says nothing familiar looked like this. The report was posted to NUFORC on October 24.

A trick of sun and distance, or a capsule that flew into a door that should not have been there?

Source: https://nuforc.org/sighting/?id=201648

Holly, Michigan. October 8, 2026, about 9:15 PM.

A driver pulled up the driveway and, for a moment, the sky looked empty. Then a triangular object with three bright white lights was already there, moving incredibly fast to the southeast.

The witness later told NUFORC the craft looked about fifty feet between the lights, dark purple or black, clearly blocking the sky behind it, with no red or green navigation lights and no flashing beacons. There was no sound. It seemed low at first, then climbed fast. By the time the car was stopped, the phone was out, and the door was open, the triangle was already a single light in the distance. The whole clear view lasted maybe thirty to forty five seconds.

FlightRadar24, which the witness uses regularly for plane spotting, showed nothing that matched. The report was posted to NUFORC on October 21.

A stealth aircraft nobody filed a flight plan for, or something that was never on the board?

New Albany, Indiana. The New Albany Sugar Shoppe, downtown.

Owner Stevie Carper sells specialty bourbon balls out of a pink storefront that is also a stop on Timothy Romig's New Albany Wicked Walk. Carper says the shop has a resident ghost she calls Frederick. In local lore he was a baker, and the first person murdered in the town, killed in the basement of what is now her store. "Basically, Frederick was the first person to be murdered in our town. I don't really see him so much, I feel him," she told WDRB in October.

Carper and Romig say they have never felt threatened by whatever is in the building. They tell the story as local history, with her permission, on a tour Romig has run since 2019.

This fall the story spilled into a fight over who gets to tell it. Carper says U.S. Ghost Adventures, a national company with tours in hundreds of cities, listed the Sugar Shoppe, used photos of the shop and its logo, and told Frederick's story on its New Albany Ghost Tours site without asking her first. She says she left a message asking them to remove her information, they said they would, and the listing stayed up. Romig says other small town guides have warned him the same thing is happening elsewhere. A request for comment from the company had not been returned in the local coverage.

Ghost in the basement, or a fight over who owns a town's ghost stories?

Source: https://www.wdrbwave.com/2026/10/23/new-albany-shop-owner-accuses-national-ghost-tour-company-using-story-without-permission/

Johnstown, Pennsylvania. Singer Hill Road, late July 1989, about 3:30 PM.

A young woman who worked at a Johnstown radio station did not have a car, so her father drove her in and she walked the roughly six miles home. It was an unusually hot day. She changed out of her work clothes, put a mixed tape in her Walkman, and headed down Singer Hill toward the city. The road was heavily wooded on both sides.

Farther from the houses, she got the feeling she was being watched. She heard a knock on the metal guardrail, pulled off her headphones, and told herself the heat was making the metal expand. Then another knock, farther ahead and downhill. She walked faster. Then she smelled the worst smell of her life, nowhere near the dead skunk she had passed that morning.

Across the street and up the hill, trees started moving left and right as if something was pushing them aside. A tall, huge shadow stopped running and ducked down. She saw white fur, then locked eyes with whatever was looking back at her. She ran.

At her brother's house she was hysterical. About half an hour later he drove her back up Singer Hill. In that short window the clear hot day had turned dark and stormy, and rain had washed the hillside and the road. Any footprints were gone. She kept the story mostly to family until she filed it with the BFRO decades later, after hearing about knocks on a Bigfoot show and realizing the guardrail sounds might not have been the heat.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=84713

Colfax, Washington. St. Ignatius Hospital.

Built in 1893 as Whitman County's first hospital, later an assisted living home, and abandoned after 2003, the brick complex on the hill has spent the last decade as one of the Northwest's best known haunted sites. Historical daytime tours and night flashlight hunts brought tens of thousands of visitors to the farming town, and the ticket money was what paid for restoration.

Then, in October 2026, the busiest month of the year, Washington Labor and Industries shut the tours down. A neighbor who had already been trespassed after harassing a guide filed a safety complaint. Investigators focused on debris and whether hazardous materials had been handled without a proper Good Faith Inspection. Sold out October weekends were cancelled and refunded. A roof repair already underway suddenly had no tour income behind it.

Owner Austin Storm says visitor safety was always taken seriously and that the process can be worked through. Guide Val has called the building one of the top haunted locations in the country. Skeptics hear an old hospital with peeling paint and a paperwork fight. Believers hear a place that still will not stay quiet, now locked by the state instead of by a spirit.

Source: https://www.khq.com/news/safety-complaint-pauses-tours-at-haunted-st-ignatius-hospital-in-colfax/article_53e6ab58-279d-47e7-b4f7-37c309e67c2d.html

Mattoon, Illinois. September 1944. A small wartime town woke up to a sweet smell at the window, then panic.

Top 5 things to know about the Mad Gasser of Mattoon:

1) On the night of September 1, 1944, a Mattoon couple reported a sickly sweet odor in their bedroom, then burning mouths, nausea, and temporary paralysis in the legs. Similar calls started stacking up across town.

2) Over about two weeks, local papers logged more than two dozen reports of a mysterious gas sprayed at windows and doors, often blamed on a thin figure in dark clothes seen running from the house.

3) Victims described the same pattern: a sweet chemical smell, then dizziness, vomiting, and legs that would not move for up to thirty or forty minutes, while police raced from porch to porch.

4) Mattoon police and health officials never caught an attacker. By mid September the official line leaned on mass hysteria, wartime nerves, and industrial odors drifting from a local plant.

5) Researchers still split. Some see a classic mid century panic. Others argue a real prowler used a homemade anesthetic and got away while the town argued with itself.

A phantom with a spray gun, or a town that gaslit its own fear?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_Gasser_of_Mattoon

Big Sur, California. Along the Santa Lucia Mountains, hikers keep reporting tall silhouettes on the ridges at dusk.

Top 5 things to know about the Dark Watchers:

1) For generations, people along the Big Sur coast have described featureless dark figures standing on the Santa Lucia ridgelines, often at dawn or dusk, sometimes wearing what looks like a hat and a long cloak, sometimes holding a walking stick.

2) The figures are said to watch in silence. When a hiker waves, calls out, or tries to close the distance, the silhouette vanishes, as if it was never solid in the first place.

3) John Steinbeck wrote them into his 1938 story "Flight," and poet Robinson Jeffers nodded to the same ridge watchers, which helped push a local story into California literary lore.

4) Similar reports stretch back through Spanish and Chumash era storytelling in the region, always tied to those high, foggy coastal mountains rather than a single town street.

5) Skeptics favor an optical explanation, especially the Brocken spectre, a giant shadow of the observer thrown onto mist at the right sun angle, plus ordinary ridge silhouettes in low light. Believers say that does not cover every calm, clear evening report.

Shadows on the fog, or something that has been standing on those ridges longer than the hiking trails?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_Watchers

Joplin, Missouri. October 12, 2026, about 3:25 PM.

A husband, wife, and daughter were driving the interstate when they saw a highly reflective metallic object ahead, low enough that they first guessed it was a mylar balloon. As they got closer, at maybe forty to a hundred feet up, it was traveling across the highway at roughly twenty five to thirty five miles per hour. Then it slowed and hovered.

What happened next is the part that does not fit a balloon. The object, only a few feet long when stretched out, began morphing. It contorted, spiraled, and seemed to turn inside out without breaking its surface, more like a fluid mass than a craft. Three orange lights appeared and vanished as the shape folded. The family watched for about a minute before the highway carried them past.

The witness says he and his wife usually look for ordinary explanations. This time the hovering, the topology change, and the lights left them without one. He later noticed similar behavior in a viral Oaxaca clip, which he says he had never seen before that day.

Newly released FAA records, obtained by John Greenewald Jr. of The Black Vault, show that multiple airline pilots reported a mysterious object near the runway during the busy Labor Day travel window. On the air traffic control recording, one speaker compared the reflective shape to a silver sphere.

A San Diego County Sheriff's ASTREA helicopter also reportedly saw the object but could not get video. At least seven aircraft filed reports. Departures were suspended. By evening, about 420 flights had been delayed.

Nearby, Naval Air Station North Island contacted controllers about an unauthorized drone the military was preparing to engage. A separate ATC remark suggested something near North Island may have been shot down. That claim remains unverified. No public military documentation confirms a shoot down or a recovery.

Tuscaloosa, Alabama. The Jemison-Van de Graaff Mansion.

Finished in 1862 as Senator Robert Jemison Jr.'s weekend townhome, it was the most technologically advanced house in the state at the time, the first fully lit with gas and the first with a fully working indoor bathroom. Today Historic Tuscaloosa keeps it open, and the building still collects stories.

Visitors and staff talk about creaks, unexplained breezes, and orbs in the rooms. The story that sticks is about a child who died in the house, and a soft aura glow that people say still appears on the main staircase. There is also one violent death on the record. Colonel Hargrove took his own life in the house after a Civil War bullet lodged in the back of his head left him with crushing headaches.

Will Hawkins, executive director of Historic Tuscaloosa, is careful with the lore. He points to old wood and old history. He also admits that when he is the last one out at night, he tells Mrs. Jemison good night, just to be sure everybody in the house is still happy.

Source: https://www.wvtm13.com/article/haunted-alabama-tuscaloosas-jemison-van-de-graaff-mansion/74278576

St. Maries, Idaho. Benewah County. October 20, 2026, about 5 PM.

A deer hunter was alone on an evening hunt about ten miles southeast of town, walking a trail through thick pine forest toward a creek bottom. From what sounded like two or three hundred yards away in the creek bed, he heard loud knocking on a tree. Immediately after, a super strong smell of death washed over him.

The knocking went on for five to ten minutes. He searched for any carcass that could explain the smell and found nothing. No dead animal. No human footprints. No other trucks on the road into that drainage all day. He also heard, briefly, what sounded like a really deep voice, a kind of gibberish he could not make out as words.

He is a seasoned outdoorsman who usually hunts in Bonner County and says he has never had what he would call a potential sasquatch encounter before. Conditions were calm, clear skies, dusk. The smell, he wrote, was as strong as if he were standing right on top of a carcass, and he could not find a single sign of one.

Midlothian, Illinois. Bachelor's Grove Cemetery, in the Rubio Woods Forest Preserve.

This small graveyard sits in the trees just off the remains of the old Midlothian Turnpike, an acre set aside in 1864 for a settler cemetery. The last burial was in 1989, and since the 1970s it has drawn ghost hunters, legend trippers and partygoers. Vandals left few of its original markers standing, and the stories grew around a campfire: floating lights, phantom cars, ghostly figures in the woods.

The most famous story has a date. On August 10, 1991, members of the Ghost Research Society were photographing the cemetery with black and white infrared film near a nameless stone marked only with a checkerboard pattern, where they said their equipment was acting up. Nobody was seen there. When the print was enlarged, it showed a young woman in an old fashioned dress sitting on the stone, parts of her body semi transparent. The Chicago Sun-Times ran it, and she became the Madonna of Bachelor's Grove.

Then there is the debate. Local historian Brad Bettenhausen says few of the cemetery's tales "have any apparent basis in fact." Skeptics still favor a double exposure, or a real person made to look see through by infrared film. Defenders say photographers ruled that out, but no written report was ever published, and the original negative has never been independently tested.

A lonely ghost on a checkerboard stone, or the most famous trick of the light in Illinois?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor%27s_Grove_Cemetery

Sandusky, Ohio. Look out over Lake Erie at dusk long enough, and locals will tell you about Bessie.

Top 5 things to know about Bessie, the Lake Erie Monster:

1) Bessie, also called South Bay Bessie or simply the Lake Erie Monster, is the lake monster of northeastern Ohio and Michigan folklore. She is usually described as snake like, 30 to 40 feet long, at least a foot thick, and gray.

2) One of the oldest stories dates to 1793, when the captain of the sloop Bay Rat, shooting ducks north of Sandusky, startled a large snake like creature "more than a rod" long. In July 1817 a schooner crew reported a dark 30 to 40 foot serpent, and later that year another crew saw a copper colored one about 60 feet long and shot at it with muskets, with no visible effect.

3) Also in 1817, near Toledo, two French settler brothers named Dusseau said they found a huge creature writhing on the beach, 20 to 30 feet long and shaped like a sturgeon, but with arms. When they came back, it was gone, leaving marks in the sand and silver scales about the size of silver dollars.

4) In July 1892, the whole crew of a ship bound from Buffalo to Toledo said they watched a 50 foot "huge sea serpent" thrashing in churned up water "as if fighting with an unseen foe," its eyes "viciously sparkling." In 1896, four witnesses at Crystal Beach near Fort Erie watched a 30 foot creature with a dog shaped head for 45 minutes.

5) Sightings came back in 1969, the 1980s and 1993, and in 1990 Huron marina owner Thomas Solberg offered a $5,000 reward to anyone who captured South Bay Bessie alive. Most of the old accounts have never been verified, and skeptics point to big sturgeon, logs and waves.

A giant sturgeon, a floating log, or something still out there past the breakwall?

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_(lake_monster)

Crawfordsville, Indiana. September 1891. Something white and enormous hung over the town at night, and people would not stop talking about it.

Top 5 things to know about the Crawfordsville Monster:

1) On September 5, 1891, the Crawfordsville Journal reported that two ice delivery men saw "a horrible apparition" hovering in the air above them that "filled them with dread." A Methodist pastor and his wife reported seeing it too.

2) The paper described it as about 18 feet long and 8 feet wide, pure white, like "a great white shroud fitted with propelling fins," with no head or tail but "one great flaming eye," and a "wheezing plaintive sound" from a mouth nobody could see. It flapped like a flag and squirmed "as though suffering unutterable agony."

3) According to interviews collected years later by local reporter Vincent Gaddis, hundreds of residents watched it the next evening, and some claimed they felt its "hot breath" as it swooped over them.

4) The story spread to the Indianapolis Journal and the Brooklyn Eagle, where it caught the eye of Charles Fort. Jerome Clark later called it "among the most fantastic of all UFO reports," and it fed early theories that some UFOs are living creatures.

5) Two local men, John Hornbeck and Abe Hernley, followed it around town and said it was a flock of many hundred killdeer. The Journal suggested the town's newly installed electric lights had confused the birds, their white undersides lit up from below.

Confused birds under new streetlights, or something that flew over Indiana and never came back?

A man was driving with his girlfriend down Scottsville Chili Road, just outside Rochester, when white lights showed up in the sky over them. Then the lights started following them.

The sighting lasted about 15 minutes, and nobody heard a sound.

Tiffin, Ohio. August 16, 2026, about 41,000 feet up.

Two pilots were flying an empty private charter jet over Ohio, getting ready to thread a gap in a wall of thunderstorms with cloud tops near 53,000 to 55,000 feet, when the captain spotted something ahead of the aircraft.

At first he thought it was a weather balloon. As they got closer, it looked like a smooth metallic pill standing vertically in the sky, the same width top to bottom, with no seams, wings, lights or control surfaces, its polished surface reflecting the evening sun. The crew put it around 43,000 feet, about 2,000 feet above them, moving on a roughly parallel but opposite course before passing off their left side. The whole encounter lasted about two minutes.

The captain called Cleveland Center and asked if controllers had any traffic or balloons in the area. They had no radar target. The jet's collision avoidance system showed nothing, and neither did his ForeFlight traffic feed.

NUFORC investigator Ben Hansen interviewed the captain and pulled the air traffic audio and FAA radar records through a FOIA request. No matching balloon launch has turned up, though a balloon has not been ruled out.

Source: https://garnerreport.com/pilots-encounter-mysterious-metallic-object-at-41000-feet/

Rockville, Indiana. The Indiana State Sanatorium.

The old tuberculosis hospital outside Rockville later served as a nursing home, and today the Sanatorium Project gives tours of its empty halls. "The word paranormal means we can't explain it. And there's a lot of things here I can't explain," business manager Steve Cecchin told News 18 this week.

One spot comes up again and again: the base of a staircase in the former TB hospital, where numerous visitors, particularly women, say they suddenly feel sick and want off the property immediately. Others report a tap on the shoulder. Some have shown Cecchin scratches they say they picked up inside.

Then there is a wing of the former nursing home known as Shadow Hallway. Visitors describe shadow figures moving room to room, some of them 10 feet tall, poking their heads out of doorways and looking out the windows. Volunteers say the patient who lived behind the second door on the right does not like all the attention. He feels like a lion in a circus.

The property carries hard history, too: a power plant engineer who reportedly shot a co-worker and then himself, and a patient who spoke of a ghostly nurse who was unkind to her, then climbed the water tower in a snowstorm and froze to death.

Manitou Springs, Colorado. December 28, 2023, about 3:25 PM.

A husband and wife had just hiked the Manitou Incline, reaching the top around 2 PM, and after a half hour break they started back down Barr Trail. By then the sunny morning had turned overcast and snowy, and the trail was nearly empty.

Where the trail opens up over the creek and the cog railway tracks, they both saw a very large, shadowy figure walking on the far side of the tracks. They stopped and looked at each other to make sure they had both seen the same thing. When they looked back, the figure had completely disappeared.

What bothered them most was the location. There is no easy way across the creek there, and no trail where the figure was walking. They waited a few minutes for it to show again. It never did.

Before leaving, they took a selfie with that spot behind them. The figure is not in the picture, only the place where it had been. It was very quiet and still, they wrote, cold and snowy. Their sons later told them the Pikes Peak area is a hot spot for sightings, and this month they made it official.

Source: https://www.bfro.net/GDB/show_report.asp?id=82711

Atchison, Kansas. The Sallie House, 508 N 2nd St.

The house dates to the mid 1800s and was commissioned by the Finney family, home to Dr. Charles Finney. Legend says he practiced medicine on the bottom floor, and that a little girl named Sallie was brought in by her mother with severe abdominal pain. Believing her appendix was about to rupture, he began emergency surgery and made the first incision before the anesthesia kicked in. Sallie screamed in pain and bled out on the table.

Tenants have reported activity for decades, especially men. Some male residents and visitors say they were scratched until they bled, which earned Sallie the name "The Man Hating Ghost." Some believe "Sallie" is only a facade for something more demonic.

Then there is the controversy. There is no physical evidence that a Sallie ever lived or died on the property, and it has been said the mayor made the story up as a publicity stunt to bring visitors to Atchison. Even the floor plan does not really fit the idea of a doctor's office downstairs. The house has been vacant since the 1990s, was listed on Zillow for $1 million in 2016, dropped to $499,000, and came off the market in 2017.

It has still been featured on Sightings, A Haunting, Paranormal Witness, Ghost Adventures in 2015, and twice on Buzzfeed Unsolved. A real ghost, a demon, or a town's best tourism pitch?

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sallie_House

London, England, 1837. A figure leaps out of a dark alley on Clapham Common, and for the next seventy years nobody can catch him.

Top 5 things to know about Spring-heeled Jack:

1) The first claimed sighting came in October 1837, when a servant girl named Mary Stevens was walking across Clapham Common in London. A figure leapt at her from a dark alley and grabbed her, and she said his claws were "cold and clammy as those of a corpse." When she screamed, he fled and could not be found.

2) The next day he reportedly jumped in front of a passing carriage, causing the coachman to crash, then escaped over a high wall while cackling with a high, ringing laugh. Soon the press and public were calling him Spring-heeled Jack.

3) Witnesses described a terrifying figure with clawed hands and eyes that "resembled red balls of fire." Some said he wore a black cloak, a helmet and a tight white garment like oilskin, and several claimed he could breathe out blue and white flames.

4) On 9 January 1838, the Lord Mayor of London, Sir John Cowan, read out an anonymous complaint from "a resident of Peckham" at a public session at the Mansion House. Letters poured in from all over London, with claims that young women had been frightened into fits and wounded by his claws, and police were told to search for him.

5) Sightings spread across the United Kingdom, especially suburban London, the Midlands and Scotland, and the last reported sighting is said to have come in Liverpool in 1904. Theories range from a prankster to something stranger, and he became the star of serials and works of fiction.

Prankster in a costume or something that really could clear a wall in one jump? Nobody ever caught him.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring-heeled_Jack

Paulding, Michigan. Park at the end of Robbins Pond Road after dark, look down the valley, and wait for the light.

Top 5 things to know about the Paulding Light:

1) The light appears in a valley outside Paulding, Michigan, in the Upper Peninsula near Watersmeet, off US 45 on Robbins Pond Road. It is also called the Lights of Paulding or the Dog Meadow Light, and people say it shows up nearly every night.

2) The first recorded sighting was in 1966, when a group of teenagers reported the light to the local sheriff. People have been driving out to watch for it ever since.

3) The most popular legend says the valley once had railroad tracks, and the light is the lantern of a brakeman killed trying to stop a train from hitting cars stopped on the line. Other versions say it is a slain mail courier, a Native American spirit dancing on the power lines, or a grandparent searching for a lost grandchild with a lantern that keeps needing to be relit.

4) In October 1990, investigators using telescopes, spectroscopy and travel time analysis identified it as the head and tail lights of vehicles on US 45 to the north. In 2010, Michigan Tech students in the SPIE chapter looked through a telescope and could see cars and even a specific Adopt a Highway sign, then recreated the effect by driving that stretch of road.

5) Not everyone is satisfied. Skeptic Ben Radford says similar lights show up all over the country with many possible causes, and that "it's more fun to imagine the distant glimmer is a ghostly railroad brakeman's phantom lantern than the headlights of a 2005 Honda Civic."

Ghost lantern or Honda Civic? The valley is still there, and so is the light.

Learn more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulding_Light

Valentine, Nebraska. Centennial Hall, the old schoolhouse built in 1897.

The two story red brick building sits on 20 inch thick foundation walls cut from local white stone. Back then the press said Valentine had built a school that "fire, wind, water or even time will be unable to destroy." Locals say something else never left either.

The stories center on Lila May Benham, a 17 year old schoolgirl who died of "heart trouble" in Valentine in 1944, newspaper clips confirm. Around town, her story comes with a poisoned clarinet reed.

Around 2012, after midnight, Dean Jacobs stood inside the old schoolhouse with a ghost hunting crew. They heard rhythmic knocks in the walls from an unseen hand, saw lights flicker on command, and a sweeping radio spoke Jacobs' name.

"That place is haunted," Preston Stoeger told reporters this fall. He described screams, footsteps and doors slamming with no explanation, and says the gym next door is the real haunted building. Two reporters spent a night inside to find out.

Source: https://www.hastingstribune.com/locals-claim-130-year-old-centennial-hall-in-valentine-is-haunted-by-ghost-of-a/article_cb6f38ed-28c3-4a54-adc5-0784902c5808.html

Phoenix, New York. October 10, 2026, around 9:50 PM.

A witness who lists themselves as a law enforcement officer filed a report with NUFORC after letting their dogs out into the backyard. Stepping onto the back deck, they looked northwest and saw a bright orange orb of light streaking across the sky.

Then it split into four smaller orange orbs. The four lined up in a straight line across the sky, equal distances apart, and moved north together in formation, faster than a plane but slower than a shooting star.

Then they faded one at a time, starting with the far left orb and moving right, until the last one went dark. The whole thing lasted about 10 seconds. The report notes a haze around the lights, that the object emitted other objects, and that animals reacted.

One light became four, and four became nothing.

Palatka, Florida. Elsie Bell's antique store, 111 N. Fourth St.

The building once housed Johnson Funeral Home, and the stories at Elsie Bell's center on Edgar Johnson, a former director there. Dealers and clerks have reported a shadowy figure standing quietly off to the side or near the cash register at closing time, dressed in an old fashioned black mourning suit with a white pocket handkerchief.

Doors left closed at night turn up ajar in the morning. A vacuum cleaner has run on its own. Tools and merchandise show up in places nobody left them. A book of ghost stories kept turning up on the floor every morning until someone finally bought it.

One dealer grabbed the back door key just after opening, went to unload, and came back to the front frightened after seeing a man in a back room. A clerk checked and found no one, but boxes and heavy furniture in front of a closet had been moved and the closet door stood open. Shown old photographs, the dealer picked out the man he saw. It was Edgar Johnson's twin brother.

"Edgar is still there," local historian Deputy said. "He has been seen many, many times."
